title: Public ZTF data show a constant AT2023uqm period while its flare fluence grew 1.6-fold per flare; one energy-proportional clock for three periodic nuclear transients fails only for some markers
abstract: Question: do the flare clocks of the three best-timed periodic nuclear transients (ASASSN-14ko, eRASSt J0456-20, AT2023uqm) follow one law in which the orbit loses energy in proportion to the radiated flare energy? Approach: we measured the five AT2023uqm flares again in public ZTF data-release light curves (2018-2025), with a seeing-dependent host model and two-Gaussian flare fits. For each source we fitted timing models with free jitter, including an energy-coupled clock (each passage changes the period by -k times its flare energy). A Monte Carlo over black-hole mass, stellar mass and bolometric energy converted k to Q, the orbital energy lost per passage over the radiated energy, and a simulation-calibrated likelihood-ratio test checked one common Q. Results: our AT2023uqm markers agree with the published markers within 0.0-2.7 d. The fluence grows by 1.59 +/- 0.07 per flare (r), but the period change per passage is +0.03 +/- 0.80 d (first peak) or +0.8 +/- 1.1 d (dip), and k is consistent with zero. The first peak moves earlier relative to the dip by 1.3 +/- 0.4 d per flare, so the period depends on the marker (524.45 to 527.06 d). For J0456-20 the energy-coupled clock fits cycles 1-5 as well as the best broken clock and forecasts cycles 6-7 with |z| <= 1.7 (X-ray weights). For ASASSN-14ko it is worse than a break in the period derivative. Q is 0.025 (95%: 0.003-0.21) for ASASSN-14ko and 0.023 (0.001-0.47) for J0456-20 (black-hole mass 1e7); these agree (p = 0.79). AT2023uqm disagrees with each of them for the dip marker (p = 0.015, 0.007); the three-source test gives p = 0.025 for the dip, but 0.11 with 2 d of extra jitter and 0.25 for the first peak. Q << 1 everywhere, so orbital energy does not power the flares. Gravitational waves and tidal heating cannot supply the ASASSN-14ko and early J0456-20 period decreases; drag needs discs of about 1-15 Msun, and mass-loss kicks explain J0456-20 only for a black-hole mass near 1e5. Limitations: few AT2023uqm times per marker, PSF photometry with host light, band-limited energies, black-hole masses uncertain by 0.3-2 dex, and no public data for the 2026 flares.

display.caption: AT2023uqm in the public ZTF data release: nightly nuclear excess flux in g and r after a seeing-dependent host model, with the five flares and our two-Gaussian fits. Flare 1 is not resolved into two peaks in the base fit; flare 3 is sparse; the first peak of flare 5 fell in the seasonal gap.

Left: AT2023uqm timing markers (published and this work) relative to a 526.75-d ephemeris; orange lines show the dip times that the energy coupling of ASASSN-14ko would predict. Right: flare fluence grows by 1.59 +/- 0.07 per flare in r while the period stays constant.

Left: coupling Q (orbital energy lost per passage over radiated flare energy) for each source, with Monte Carlo 68% and 95% ranges. Right: marginal likelihood of a common Q (base case, dip marker; p = 0.025). ASASSN-14ko and J0456-20 agree; AT2023uqm prefers Q near zero.
